events.text:
This is game 1 in a series of 9×9 Go games. Each new game starts in a fresh session.

## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If CLAUDE.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session; your other files are there to read with the file tools. What a later session knows of your earlier games is what you have left in these files.

Your working directory is empty.

## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- `clear_context()` asks for a fresh session for this same game. After calling it, end your turn; the new session starts like this one, with your files and the game where you left it, and without this conversation.
- Files: your Read, Write, Edit, Glob and Grep tools, for any file in your working directory.

You also have a shell, and you may write and run code in it. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over, unless you use `clear_context()`. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
For the first game, I should pick an opponent rank to calibrate difficulty—starting around 8k seems like a reasonable gauge before adjusting.

I'm tracking the liberties around F9 and F8, checking whether playing G8 puts F8 in atari without actually connecting to F9's remaining liberty at G9, since G8 isn't adjacent to F9.

Testing F7 instead: this puts F8 in atari with only G8 as a liberty. If white responds by extending to G8, or by capturing F9 with G9, I'm tracing out the resulting liberty counts for each group to see which continuation leaves black stronger, and it's getting tangled since the E9/D9 chain adds extra liberties that complicate a clean capture sequence.

Following this further, white does pick up F9,G9,F8 but it's a small, contained loss since black's F7-E7-E8 group keeps libs at E6, G7, F6. I try the alternative of white extending to G8 instead, but it still just leads to white gaining a few stones along the edge while black connects fine — overall this looks like an acceptable, minor concession for black.

Checking: after white F7, if black tries F9 to recapture it's suicide since all neighbors are white with no new libs, so black must play G8 instead, letting white connect at F9 — leaving white solid at F8/F9/G9 against black G8/F7/H9. I'm also weighing whether black should just play G9 now and accept the F7 atari on E7-E8 instead.

But actually E7-E8 isn't in trouble — if white atari with F7, black can connect out via E6, which links to the D6/E5 group and saves everything. That leaves white's F7-F8 stones stuck inside black's area with only three liberties, weak and isolated beneath black's F9-G9 wall — a much better outcome for black than chasing the G8 fight.

If white connects out via the left side, the group lives, and black only loses a bit of the top-right corner — still a tolerable trade with a solid H8-G7-F7 wall. The alternative of black playing G9 is clearly worse, so I'll just settle on F7.

# Go series notes (read first)

## Results log
- Game 1: vs 8k, Black. LOST (resigned at move ~59). Was already behind ~10 by area count.

## Lessons (most important first)
1. **Count liberties of MY OWN groups before every move**, especially edge groups
   like a chain along row 1-2. In game 1 my bottom chain B1-F2 had only 2 libs
   (F1, F2-side); white invaded F3/E3 then G2 and the chain died in atari. Before
   answering an invasion, list libs of every adjacent black group.
2. **Count the score early (around move 20)**. Area count = stones + surrounded
   empty. In game 1 I thought I was ahead after the opening but was actually
   behind ~6: White's two 3rd-line stones (C3, C6) + solid left side were worth
   more than my right side, and komi is 7.
3. Opening: E5 then G4 let White take the whole left side cheaply (C3, C6).
   Consider responding closer / blocking white's second stone (e.g. approach
   between them early) instead of a slow extension.
4. Cutting moves deep in the opponent's area (C5 cut, C7 cut, B4) mostly just
   lost stones vs 8k — the engine answers locally correctly. Don't count on
   blunders; 8k KataGo reads short tactics fine.
5. Hane at the 1st/2nd line (D1, F9) created weaknesses that White exploited
   (F9 stone captured, F8 push). Be careful with hanes that leave cutting points.

## Opponent ladder plan
- 8k was too strong for my game-1 play. Try 10k-12k next game; move up after a win.
